headline: Niantic Fleet Finds Bass Locked On Bunker at Black Point — Fluke Grade Slipping Deeper
subhead: The new moon push pinned bait tight against Twotree Channel and Hole-in-the-Wall, and the stripers finally committed hard.
body_markdown:
Dock talk at the Niantic Bay landing this week has been all bunker, all the time. Mates working the drift boats have been calling in bait schools stacked so heavy against the beach at Black Point and up through Twotree Island Channel that the sounders are showing solid red from the surface down to fifteen, twenty feet. That's the September 10 new moon doing exactly what it's supposed to do this time of year — the tidal swing that came with it was the hardest push of the early fall season, and it squeezed those bunker schools tight against the shoreline structure from the Niantic River mouth out through Hole-in-the-Wall.

We flagged this building last week — said the bass were in that classic staging pattern, picking at stragglers but not yet committing, and that it would tip over once the bait got pinned down under the moon. That's exactly what's happening now. The fleet went from marking scattered fish under bait to putting bent rods in the boat on every drift through the bunker schools. New London's holding around 69.4, which is still comfortable water, but it's cooling fast enough that everything in the food chain knows the calendar's turning.

The pattern that's working: live-lined bunker on light circle hooks, snagged fresh off the schools and dropped right back down into the same pod. Boats are working the last two hours of the ebb, when the tide pulls bait out of the Niantic River and stacks it against the drop-off on the Twotree Channel side — that current seam is holding fish 15 to 25 feet down, and the bigger stripers are sitting under the bait rather than busting through the top of it. Where the blitzes do break the surface, especially in the last hour of light off Black Point, swim shads in bunker colors and 2-ounce bucktails worked with a slow lift-and-drop are getting bit just as well as the live stuff, without the hassle of snagging bait boat-side.

Fluke's a different story, and it's worth being straight about it. The keeper-grade bite that was solid through August has thinned out. Most of what's coming over the rail in the shallower water — the flats off McCook Point, the inside edges of Niantic Bay — is short fish, one and two inches under. The better grade has done what better fluke do this time of year: they've slid off into deeper, cooler water ahead of their fall exit offshore. Locally that means working the deeper cuts off Twotree Channel and the mouth of Niantic Bay in 25 to 35 feet instead of the shallow sand. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow on the drift, are still finding the occasional keeper down there, but the ratio of shorts to keepers has flipped hard in favor of the shorts. If fluke is the main target this weekend, put the time in deeper and expect to cull through some undersized fish before a keeper shows.

Sea bass have actually picked up, which tracks with the same cooling trend that's chasing the fluke deeper — that water easing back into the mid-to-upper 60s is right in the comfort zone for bottom fish. Black Point's rock piles and the ledges around Hole-in-the-Wall are holding decent grade sea bass in 20 to 35 feet. Bucktail jigs tipped with squid strips or a chunk of clam, bounced right on the structure, are getting bit steady — nothing spectacular in size, but a consistent fifteen-fish morning isn't hard to put together right now if you're willing to move around the rock piles instead of anchoring on one spot.

Porgies are still doing their reliable September thing on the bottom in Twotree Channel, 20 to 30 feet, on clam and squid strips fished on a simple high-low rig. Nothing glamorous, but it's steady action for anyone bringing kids out or just wanting a full cooler.

Bluefish are the sleeper story right now. Snapper blues are thick in the Niantic River and up into the shallow flats of Niantic Bay — that's usually the tell that bigger blues aren't far behind as the water keeps cooling, and the fleet's already seeing some adult bluefish mixed right into the bass blitzes at Black Point, hitting bunker chunks and cut bait fished on wire leaders behind the live-lining spread. Worth having a second rod rigged for blues if you're working bunker schools, because they're showing up uninvited and they're not shy about it.

Looking at the next few days, the tide's still carrying real push behind it as the moon works its way off new phase, so expect the Black Point and Twotree Channel bass pattern to hold, particularly on the early outgoing tide when bait gets funneled out of the river and pinned against the channel edge. Wind is the variable to watch — if it stays out of the north or northwest, the water should stay clean and the bite should hold through the week. If it swings southwest and builds, that could push and color the water inside the bay, which would push the better window back to first light before the wind fills in. Best case, this bunker push holds another week or two before it thins out and pushes offshore with the fluke — that's usually how the pattern runs into October around here. Worth getting out while the bait's still pinned tight against the beach.
